overview.text: Marble is a metamorphic rock, usually formed when limestone is altered by heat and pressure: its calcite recrystallizes into interlocking crystals, commonly obscuring fossils and earlier textures. Though often white or pale, mineral impurities can create colored bands and veins. The crystalline stone can be carved to fine detail, lets light pass through slightly, and can be polished to a sheen—qualities that helped make it prized for statues, buildings, and monuments. In ancient Greece, marble was used extensively in architecture and sculpture from the seventh century BCE onward; sculptors polished it and often added paint, so ancient statues were not necessarily plain white.

key_facts.text: Marble is made mostly of calcite, a calcium-carbonate mineral; when dolostone undergoes metamorphism, it can form dolomitic marble.
Recrystallization produces interlocking crystals and can obscure the fossils and sedimentary textures of the original limestone.
Marble is often white when its source limestone has few impurities; other minerals can give it gray, pink, yellow, or darker colors.
White marble was valued for its slight translucence and ability to hold finely carved detail; marble can also be polished to a high luster.
The Met notes that Greek builders and sculptors used marble extensively from the seventh century BCE onward; its surfaces were often polished and painted.
